narration.text: Nine thousand years ago, in a village in central China, someone made a flute from the wing bone of a crane.
It can still be played.
Along two great rivers, people began to farm. Millet by the Yellow River, in the north. Rice along the Yangtze, in the south.
And they learned to unwind a silk moth's cocoon into one long, shining thread.
More than three thousand years ago, Shang kings ruled the Yellow River plain, and cast great vessels of bronze.
To question their ancestors, they held a red-hot rod to bones and turtle shells, and read the cracks.
Then they carved the question, and the answer, beside them.
It is the oldest Chinese writing we know, and many of its signs can still be read today.
Far to the southwest, at Sanxingdui, others cast bronze faces with eyes on stalks.
The Zhou kings who came next claimed the Mandate of Heaven: a right to rule, which heaven could take away.
As their power faded, rival states fought for five hundred years.
And thinkers argued about how to live. Confucius taught respect, learning, and duty to family.
Daoists said: be like water, which yields to everything, and wears away stone.
And Sunzi wrote that the greatest victory is the one won without a fight.
In 221 BCE, the king of Qin conquered the last of his rivals, and named himself the First Emperor.
He decreed one script, one coinage, one set of weights, even one width for every cart's axle.
He joined older walls into one long wall in the north.
And he was buried with an army of clay: thousands of soldiers, no two faces alike.
Farmers found them in 1974, digging a well.
His dynasty lasted fifteen years.
The Han dynasty that followed lasted four hundred years. Most Chinese people still call themselves Han.
The envoy Zhang Qian crossed the deserts to the west, and trade followed, along the Silk Road.
Silk went west. Horses, grapes and glass came east, and later, Buddhism.
Han craftsmen made paper, from bark, hemp and old rags. This whole little world is made of it.
And Zhang Heng built a jar to detect distant earthquakes: a ball would drop from a dragon's mouth into a toad's.
An old novel begins: the empire, long divided, must unite; long united, must divide.
After the Han, it stayed divided for almost four hundred years, and Buddhism took root.
The Sui reunited it, and dug the Grand Canal, still the longest in the world.
Officials were chosen by written exams, a system that would last thirteen hundred years.
Under the Tang, the capital, Chang'an, held perhaps a million people, and merchants from as far as Persia.
Wu Zetian became the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name.
And Li Bai wrote a poem that every child in China still knows.
Moonlight before my bed. I took it for frost on the ground. I raise my head to the bright moon, and lower it, thinking of home.
Under the Song, cities boomed, and so did invention.
Alchemists looking for the elixir of eternal life had found gunpowder instead.
The Song made it into rockets, and fireworks.
Sailors steered by compass. Merchants paid with paper money.
And Bi Sheng printed with movable type, four hundred years before Gutenberg.
In 1279, the Mongols conquered all of China, and Kublai Khan ruled from where Beijing stands today.
Ninety years later, a peasant who had been a begging monk drove them out, and founded the Ming.
The Ming built the Forbidden City, and most of the Great Wall that people walk on today.
From 1405, Admiral Zheng He sailed seven times, with hundreds of ships, as far as East Africa.
One voyage brought back a giraffe. The court took it for a qilin, a creature of legend.
In 1644, the Manchus took Beijing, and founded the last dynasty, the Qing.
With new crops from the Americas, the population grew past four hundred million.
Europe craved Chinese tea, silk and porcelain, and paid in silver.
To win the silver back, British merchants smuggled in opium. When China destroyed it, Britain went to war, and won.
More wars, unequal treaties, and a civil war that killed tens of millions shook the empire.
In 1912, the last emperor gave up the throne. He was six years old.
The young republic was torn by warlords and civil war, and, from 1937, by invasion from Japan.
At least fourteen million Chinese people died.
In 1949, the Communists under Mao Zedong won, and founded the People's Republic.
Schools and clinics reached the villages, and lives grew longer.
But the Great Leap Forward, Mao's rush to industrialise, caused a famine that killed tens of millions.
In the Cultural Revolution, students were turned against their teachers, and children against their parents.
Even then, following a clue in a medical book sixteen hundred years old, Tu Youyou's team found a new cure for malaria. It has saved millions of lives.
From 1978, under Deng Xiaoping, China opened to the world, and to markets.
Shenzhen grew from a small border town into a city of almost eighteen million.
Some eight hundred million people escaped extreme poverty: the largest escape from poverty in history.
In 1989, protests in Tiananmen Square were crushed by the army.
And light reached the farthest villages. By 2015, almost every home had electricity.
Today, 1.4 billion people live in China.
Its high-speed railways, the first opened in 2008, now run for more than fifty thousand kilometres: more than the rest of the world together.
In 2019, a Chinese probe made the first landing on the far side of the Moon. In 2024, another brought back the first rocks from there.
China burns more coal than any other country, and builds about half the world's new solar and wind power.
And its forests now cover a quarter of the land, twice as much as forty years ago.
From a bone flute to the far side of the Moon, it is one long thread.
Ahead, the paper is still blank. The next part has not been written yet.
